plot_extraction.response_text:
On his last day in England before returning to his modest fruit farm in Rhodesia, insecure and financially struggling Reginald resolves to propose to Anne, a wealthy, beautiful young woman he deeply loves. After escaping his possessive widowed mother, he visits Anne and confesses his feelings.

Anne rejects him, explaining that although she likes him more than anyone else and can tell him anything, she cannot marry a man who constantly makes her laugh. Comparing them to her pet doves—where the female runs laughing ahead while the male follows, bowing—she insists such a relationship would be wrong in real life. Heartbroken, Reginald tries to leave, but Anne cannot bear his unhappiness and repeatedly calls him back. Finally, she addresses him as “Mr. Dove,” implicitly accepting the very relationship she had rejected, and he returns to her.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a close third-person perspective that remains tightly aligned with Reggie’s consciousness. The narration repeatedly slips into free indirect discourse, allowing his anxious, self-deprecating thoughts to colour the prose without formal attribution. Exclamations such as “Here he was!”, “Good heavens!” and “Dash it all” sound simultaneously like narration and private speech. This creates intimacy while preserving enough narrative distance for gentle irony: Reggie experiences his proposal as an almost tragic ordeal, while the reader also sees the social awkwardness, melodrama and comic incongruity of his behaviour.

The tone blends romantic pathos with comedy of manners. Reggie’s emotional pain is treated sympathetically, but his earnestness is continually undercut by small humiliations: the apparently green hair, the violently ringing bell, the check tie, the intimidating gardening scissors and his fervent claim to like doves. The comedy is affectionate rather than cruel. Even Anne’s laughter is presented as involuntary and mysterious, so the rejection remains emotionally complicated rather than simply callous. This tonal instability—moving from amusement to tenderness, embarrassment and hurt—is central to the story’s effect.

The diction is colloquial, class-marked and distinctly period-specific. Reggie’s idiom includes expressions such as “top-hole,” “dashed,” “mater,” “chap,” “governor,” “fearfully” and “cutting off.” These establish an upper-middle-class or minor-gentry English social world while revealing his boyishness and emotional limitations. His language relies on euphemism, understatement and unfinished formulations; he often cannot state what he feels directly until the proposal forces him to do so. Anne’s speech is softer and apparently more assured, but it too becomes fragmented when emotion threatens her composure. Social politeness therefore acts both as a shared code and as an obstacle to honest communication.

The syntax imitates the movement of thought. Long, accumulating sentences reproduce Reggie’s obsessive weighing of disadvantages, especially through repeated constructions such as “in spite of.” These are interspersed with fragments, abrupt questions, exclamations and ellipses that register hesitation and panic. Dashes are especially prominent, marking interruptions, qualifications, emotional recoil and thoughts that cannot be completed. Repetition intensifies feeling—“I love her, I love her,” “bowing and bowing,” “Roo-coo-coo-coo”—while also creating comic and symbolic patterns. The prose often advances by association rather than formal exposition, moving fluidly from physical action to memory, fantasy and imagined dialogue.

Characterisation is indirect and highly economical. Reggie is revealed through gestures—adjusting his tie, pressing against the chest of drawers, crushing out a cigarette, waving away his distress—as much as through explicit description. His lack of confidence appears in his bodily awkwardness and habitual self-belittling. His romantic imagination is cinematic and conventional: he pictures himself protecting Anne on a journey and imagines her ideal husband as a handsome theatrical stranger. Anne is characterised through laughter, small physical movements, shifting expressions and contradictions between what she says and what she does. Her wish to reject Reggie while keeping him emotionally unharmed exposes a mixture of affection, vanity, innocence and possessiveness.

Dialogue is naturalistic but carefully patterned around evasion and failed understanding. Characters interrupt themselves, repeat phrases, change subjects and speak past one another. Reggie interprets Anne’s refusal as final, whereas Anne cannot accept the emotional consequences of giving it. Her insistence that he must become “just as happy as” before is both naïve and controlling. The closing summons, “Come back, Mr. Dove,” converts the earlier metaphor into direct address and shows that the relationship she rejects in theory is the very pattern she recreates in practice.

Sensory description is vivid, selective and often filtered through emotion. The post-rain landscape is rendered through gleaming roads, briar-scented hedges, glowing hollyhocks, falling drops, petals and pollen. Interiors are similarly composed from a few resonant objects: a parasol on the piano, a green ashtray, a pearl ring catching flame. Colour is prominent—blue and cream, gold-brown, green, pink, wet blue—and lends the prose a delicate, impressionistic quality. These visual details are not static decoration; they flare into notice at moments of heightened consciousness. Immediately after Reggie asks his question, for example, the garden seems to “open to the light,” then fades with Anne’s answer.

Sound is equally important. Snipping scissors, the over-loud bell, Anne’s pealing laughter and the doves’ repeated cooing punctuate the narrative. These sounds frequently externalise Reggie’s unease or interrupt attempts at solemnity. Onomatopoeic effects such as “Snip,” “Ping!” and “Roo-coo-coo-coo” give the prose a playful, almost theatrical immediacy. Silence and pauses are also charged: the brief interval after the proposal expands into intense visual perception, slowing time at the decisive moment.

The story’s imagery depends on ironic correspondences between people, animals and objects. Reggie’s tie makes him resemble a cat in a picture; the mother’s Pekinese dogs appear to judge him; and the courting doves become the governing symbol. Mrs Dove runs ahead laughing while Mr Dove follows, endlessly bowing. Anne initially presents this as an image of the marriage she must avoid, yet her final call makes Reggie enact the same pattern. The symbol is therefore both comic and painful, encapsulating unequal affection, pursuit, submission and repetition.

The structure is compact and scene-driven. It begins with anticipatory self-scrutiny, moves through the comic obstacle of Reggie’s mother, opens into a bright transitional walk, and then concentrates almost entirely on the encounter with Anne. Pacing alternates between summary and sharply dramatised moments. Reggie’s history and prospects are compressed into rapid exposition, while the proposal and rejection unfold slowly through pauses, gestures and repeated attempts to leave. The ending is circular rather than conclusive: Reggie returns across the lawn, suggesting that the emotional pattern will continue despite the explicit refusal.

Overall, the style is psychologically intimate, impressionistic and delicately ironic. Its distinctive method is to place intense private feeling inside an outwardly trivial social episode, using colloquial free indirect narration, sensory precision, symbolic repetition and comic interruption. The result is a bittersweet study of mismatched love in which tenderness and ridicule remain inseparable, and in which the characters’ gestures reveal more than their explanations.

On the morning of his last day in England, Reginald took one look at himself in the glass and decided that his hair was green.

Not entirely green, of course. Not the green of billiard cloth or parsley sauce, but greenish where the light from the wet garden struck it above the temples. It was absurd. A man could not go and ask a girl to marry him with green hair. He leaned closer, gripping the washstand.

There! No—brown again. Rather a decent brown, perhaps, if it were not so flat. He pushed it up with both hands and instantly looked like a startled cockatoo. He smoothed it. Worse. He stepped back.

The new tie was a mistake too. The fellow in Bond Street had called it distinguished, but its checks—cream, black and an angry little line of orange—gave Reggie the appearance of a cat in one of those nursery pictures, a cat dressed for the Lord Mayor’s Show. Anne would see it at once. She saw everything. She would look at the tie, then at him, and that helpless silver laughter would begin.

Dash it all, why should a tie matter?

Because everything mattered to-day.

Here he was! His last day. At six the following morning he must take the train for Southampton, and after that came the long voyage, the hot little station, the dusty road and the fruit farm in Rhodesia, with its twelve acres of young orange trees, its unreliable pump and its mortgage. A modest property, people called it. Modest! It was practically blushing itself out of existence.

He turned sideways before the glass and drew in his stomach.

Suppose Anne accepted him. Suppose, in spite of the farm, in spite of his income being what the governor used to describe as “prospective rather than actual,” in spite of the distance and the heat and the insects, in spite of his mother, in spite of everything, she said yes. Then he would take her away. He saw them standing on the deck at night, Anne wrapped in a white cloak, the sea immensely black around them. A steward would come running up to say there was danger—fire, perhaps, or a man overboard—and Reggie, very quiet, very capable, would put Anne behind him.

“Stay there,” he would say. “Leave this to me.”

It was difficult to imagine what came next, but the effect was top-hole.

He tried the serious expression required by this scene. Unfortunately, it made his upper lip look as though it had been caught in a drawer.

“Reggie!”

His mother’s voice came from the landing.

He dropped the expression.

“Yes, mater?”

“Are you dressed?”

“Practically.”

“Then come to my room before you go down.”

That was the first obstacle.

Mrs. Fairburn sat in bed beneath a lilac satin quilt, with two Pekinese dogs beside her and the morning post spread about like fallen leaves. Widowhood had left her in possession of a large house, a small fortune and an inexhaustible sense of injury. She had been injured by the climate, by servants, by Reggie’s decision to farm abroad, by the price of asparagus, and most especially by any person who presumed to want him elsewhere.

The Pekinese dogs stared at him as he entered. Their round black eyes appeared to say that they knew precisely where he was going and thought poorly of it.

“My dear boy!” His mother raised both hands. “What have you done to your hair?”

So it was green.

“Nothing, mater.”

“You look feverish. Come here.”

“I’m all right.”

“Nonsense. Your left ear is crimson.”

Reggie put a hand to it. The dogs continued to judge him.

Mrs. Fairburn had been cutting photographs from an illustrated paper with a pair of long gardening scissors. Why gardening scissors should be in bed with her he could not imagine, but they looked fearfully sharp. Snip! went the blades through the portrait of a duchess.

“You are not going to the Harcourts’, I hope.”

“Well—I thought I might stroll over.”

“On your last day?”

“I said good-bye to everybody else yesterday.”

“Everybody else!” Snip. “I see. Your poor mother is everybody else.”

“No, no, mater. Of course not.”

“I had planned that we should spend the afternoon together. Quite quietly. You might read to me.”

The dogs brightened. No doubt they would like that—four hours of Reggie reading parliamentary speeches while they breathed on his trousers.

“I shan’t be long.”

“You always say that.”

“I must say good-bye to Anne.”

At the name, Mrs. Fairburn looked down and severed a cabinet minister at the waist.

“I cannot understand what you find so attractive in that family.”

“They’ve always been very decent to me.”

“Decent! People are decent to the postman.”

Snip.

For one dreadful moment Reggie saw himself detained until luncheon, then until tea, then until the cab arrived to take him to the station in the grey dawn. He would write to Anne from Southampton. No, from the ship. “Dear Anne, I had meant to ask you something, but mater wanted me to read aloud—”

Good heavens!

He bent and kissed his mother on the forehead.

“Sorry, mater. Absolutely must go.”

“Reggie!”

He was at the door.

“Reggie, I forbid you to—”

But he had escaped. Down the stairs, across the hall, past the maid who held out his gloves, and into the morning. Behind him the bell rang with such violence that it seemed the whole house had screamed.

The rain had stopped. The road shone, pale and glassy, beneath a rinsed blue sky. Drops fell from the elms with little separate taps, and the hedges breathed out the sweet, dark smell of briar and wet earth. Reggie walked quickly at first, almost laughing. Free! He had done it. The house receded behind him; the dogs, the scissors, the lilac quilt—all of it sank away.

Then the road curved, and beyond the wet fields he saw the Harcourts’ chimneys.

His pace slackened.

He loved Anne. That was the plain fact. He loved her, he loved her. Not because she was beautiful—though she was; not because she had money—though it would be idiotic to pretend that money did not make Rhodesia look less alarming; not because she listened to him and knew when he was trying to be amusing. He loved the way she sat on the edge of a table, swinging one foot. He loved the little crease beside her mouth when she was puzzled. He loved even her laughter, though lately it had begun to make him feel as if he were running downstairs in the dark and had missed the last step.

She liked him. Surely she did. She told him things she told nobody else: that she hated boiled milk; that her aunt’s voice made her dream of teaspoons; that once, at twelve, she had stolen a peach and buried the stone beneath her pillow from remorse. She had said he was her dearest friend.

But a girl could have a dearest friend and marry somebody else.

The somebody else appeared at once in Reggie’s mind: a tall, bronzed chap with clean-cut features and a quiet manner, a chap who entered drawing rooms without knocking over footstools. He had probably been in the cavalry. He would look at Anne as if he understood women, and his ties would never resemble cats.

“Rot,” Reggie muttered, striking a puddle with his stick.

A shower of diamonds flew into the grass. Beyond the hedge, hollyhocks glowed pink and wine-red against a cottage wall. Everything looked absurdly hopeful after the rain. The leaves flashed, the clouds sailed, a thrush shook itself and began again. It seemed impossible that on such a morning Anne could say no.

And yet she might.

At the Harcourts’ gate he stopped to adjust the tie in the tiny oval mirror of his cigarette case. Still frightful. He loosened it, tightened it, turned the knot slightly to the left and succeeded only in making the orange line more prominent.

Let it be prominent. Let it blaze. He was not proposing with his tie.

The front door stood open. Somewhere in the house a piano was being played, very softly and badly. A maid told him Miss Anne was in the garden.

“Shall I announce you, sir?”

“No, thanks. I know the way.”

He crossed the cool hall. A blue parasol lay on the piano, and beside it stood a vase of cream roses shedding petals on the polished wood. Through the open drawing-room windows came the sound of snipping.

Snipping!

For an instant he thought his mother had followed him with the gardening scissors. Then he saw Anne beyond the terrace, cutting sweet peas.

She wore a pale blue frock and a broad hat pushed back from her forehead. The wet lawn shone about her shoes. At the end of the path, two white doves strutted near a stone basin, their breasts changing from pearl to pink as they moved.

Anne looked up.

“Reggie!”

There it was—that brightness, that sudden pleased look. His heart gave one enormous thump.

“I thought you’d come.”

“Did you?”

“Of course. You couldn’t go without saying good-bye.”

“No. Rather not.”

He came down the steps. Anne held out her hand, but it was full of sweet peas; he took two of her fingers, absurdly careful not to crush them. They were cool from the stems.

“Your tie!” she said.

He knew it.

“What about it?”

“Nothing.” Her lips trembled. “It’s splendid.”

“Chap in Bond Street said so.”

“I’m sure he did.”

She turned quickly to the flowers, but a little sound escaped her. Then another. Her shoulders shook.

“Oh, Reggie, forgive me!”

“It’s all right.”

“It isn’t the tie. It’s—oh, I don’t know what it is.”

She laughed out, light and clear. The doves lifted their heads. Reggie smiled because there seemed nothing else to do, though something inside him became small and hard.

Presently Anne recovered herself and touched his sleeve.

“You don’t mind, do you?”

“Good Lord, no. Rather bucked you like it.”

“You’re so sweet.”

Sweet. A man rescuing women from burning ships was never called sweet.

They walked to a wicker table beneath the cedar. On it stood a green glass ashtray, a bowl of strawberries and a jug beaded with water. Anne dropped the sweet peas beside the bowl and sat down.

“Cigarette?”

“Thanks.”

He struck a match. Her hand curved about the flame, and the pearl in her ring caught it, turning for a second into a tiny moon. He could smell crushed grass, tobacco and the warm pollen of the flowers. It was all so vivid that he felt he would remember it in Rhodesia when everything around him was red dust and heat: Anne’s bent head, the green ashtray, a strawberry lying on its side with one white spot where it had touched the bowl.

“Well,” she said, “this time to-morrow you’ll be on the sea.”

“Not quite. Train first.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes.”

“Are you glad?”

He crushed the match into the ashtray.

“Fearfully.”

“You don’t sound glad.”

“Oh, I am. Farm and all that. Oranges coming on. Pump fixed, perhaps. Lots to do.”

“And no one to make you miserable.”

“Who makes me miserable?”

“I do, sometimes.”

“You don’t.”

“I do. I can always tell.”

She looked at him steadily. Her eyes were gold-brown, darker near the centre. Reggie’s rehearsed words—he had possessed several excellent openings on the road—vanished completely.

He had meant to begin calmly. “Anne, there’s something I’ve been wanting to say.” Or perhaps: “We’ve known each other a long time.” Instead, he heard himself ask:

“Would you hate living in Rhodesia?”

Anne’s fingers paused above the strawberries.

“I don’t know. I’ve never thought.”

“It’s not half bad. Not all snakes and savages, you know. There’s a club. Tennis. People dine out.”

“I’m sure they do.”

“And the house could be improved. Verandah wanted widening, and there’s a room at the back that could be made into—well, whatever you liked.”

Her face changed. Only a little; but he saw that she understood.

The garden seemed suddenly enormous. Beyond Anne, every leaf of the cedar stood separate against the wet blue sky. A drop slid from the stone basin. One of the doves pecked twice at the gravel.

Reggie pushed his chair back and stood.

“Anne—I say—”

She looked up at him.

He ought to take her hand. Chaps did. But her hands lay folded in her lap, so still and complete that it seemed brutal to disturb them.

“I haven’t got much,” he said. “You know that. Farm’s sound, though. At least, it will be. And I’m not much of a chap, either. Not the sort you’d naturally—what I mean is, you could marry anybody. Some top-hole fellow. But I—”

He stopped and swallowed.

Anne’s lips parted.

“I love you,” he said. “That’s the whole thing. I love you most frightfully. Will you marry me?”

Silence.

In that silence the garden opened to the light. The hollyhocks beyond the wall burned like small flags; the wet gravel glittered; a pale petal loosened from Anne’s flowers and fell upon the table. Even the doves were still.

Then Anne looked down.

“Oh, Reggie.”

The light closed.

He sat again because his knees had become unreliable.

“That means no, I suppose.”

“I’m so sorry.”

“No need to be. Perfectly all right.”

“But it isn’t all right.”

“Yes, it is. Shouldn’t have sprung it on you.”

“You didn’t spring it. I’ve known.”

“Have you?”

“Not exactly known. Felt.”

He stared at the ashtray. His cigarette had gone out. He picked it up, put it down, and brushed a thread of tobacco from his cuff.

“I like you more than anyone in the world,” Anne said.

“That’s very decent.”

“I do. There’s nobody I can talk to as I talk to you. Nobody who understands when I’m hateful. Nobody who—”

“Then why not?” He looked up. “Sorry. That sounds dashed rude. But why not?”

Anne turned towards the doves.

Mrs. Dove—the smaller bird, with a faint grey mark upon her wing—was walking briskly along the border. Mr. Dove followed. Every few steps he lowered his head and spread his tail in a white fan.

“Look at them,” Anne said.

Reggie looked.

“Rather nice.”

“Do you know what they’re doing?”

“Walking, aren’t they?”

“Watch.”

Mrs. Dove hurried on. Mr. Dove overtook her, bowed deeply and made a bubbling sound in his throat.

“Roo-coo-coo-coo.”

Mrs. Dove darted away.

Anne began to laugh.

It was not loud this time. It ran through her in small helpless ripples while Mr. Dove followed, bowing and bowing, his pink feet absurdly earnest upon the wet path.

“Roo-coo-coo-coo.”

“I don’t quite see—” Reggie began.

“That’s us.”

“Us?”

“Yes. She runs away laughing, and he comes after her and bows.”

“I don’t bow.”

“Not really. But you know what I mean.”

He did not, except that the comparison was somehow intolerable.

“And you’re always making me laugh,” she continued. “Even now—oh, don’t look like that! I don’t mean to. I can’t help it. You’re so serious, and then something happens—your tie, or the way you say a thing—and I laugh. I’d laugh all my life.”

“Cheery sort of marriage.”

“No, it wouldn’t be fair.”

“To whom?”

“To you. To either of us. A wife shouldn’t laugh at her husband.”

“Might do worse.”

“She ought to look up to him.”

“And you don’t look up to me.”

Anne pulled a petal from a sweet pea.

“You don’t want me to pretend.”

“No.”

“I love being with you. I miss you when you’re away. I can tell you everything. But marriage is different. A husband should be—”

“The cavalry fellow.”

“What cavalry fellow?”

“Nothing. Go on.”

“He should be someone one depends upon.”

“I can be depended upon.”

“I know.”

“Then that’s something.”

“Oh, Reggie, you make it impossible.”

She laughed again, but now the sound wounded her too; he could see it in the way she pressed her lips together immediately afterwards.

He rose.

“Right. Well. Thanks for letting me down lightly.”

“Don’t say that.”

“Why not? It’s what happened.”

“You’re angry.”

“Not a bit.”

“You are.”

“I’m not. I’ve no right to be.”

He found his hat on the grass and dusted it, though there was no dust. His hands looked detached from him, pale and efficient, the hands of a servant packing somebody else’s things.

“Reggie, sit down.”

“Better be cutting off.”

“Not yet.”

“Mater expects me.”

This was so monstrous a lie that even in his misery he almost admired it.

Anne stood too. “You can’t go like this.”

“Like what?”

“So unhappy.”

“I’m not unhappy.”

“You look dreadful.”

“Thanks.”

“I didn’t mean—oh, please!”

He waved his hand as if unhappiness were smoke that could be cleared from between them.

“Forget it. Absolutely forget the whole thing.”

“How can I?”

“Easy. Chap proposes, girl refuses. Happens every day.”

“But not to us.”

“Apparently it does.”

He walked towards the terrace.

“Reggie!”

He stopped.

Anne had followed him a few steps. Her face was pale beneath the hat, and the childish certainty had gone from it.

“What?”

“You mustn’t think I don’t care.”

“I don’t.”

“You do. You think I’m cruel.”

“Never thought that.”

“I couldn’t bear you to think it.”

“I don’t, Anne. Honestly.”

“Then smile.”

He smiled.

The effort drew his face into such a ghastly shape that she gave a tiny cry.

“Not like that!”

“Best I can manage at short notice.”

She held out both hands. “Come back and sit down. We’ll talk sensibly.”

“There’s nothing to talk about.”

“We can talk about the farm.”

“No.”

“About your journey, then.”

“No.”

“About anything.”

He shook his head.

“But yesterday we were happy,” she said. “We were perfectly happy.”

“Yesterday I thought you might marry me.”

“That shouldn’t make all the difference.”

“It does rather.”

“Why?”

Good heavens, how could she ask why? Because yesterday the world had contained a door and to-day she had shut it; because the garden, the house, the very road home had become things he must leave not for months but for ever; because he could not be her dearest friend while she waited for the tall chap with the flawless tie.

He said only, “That’s how it is.”

Anne’s eyes filled.

“You must be just as happy as you were before.”

“Can’t arrange it.”

“You must try.”

“Right. I’ll try in the cab.”

“Reggie!”

Again he started away. Again her voice pulled him back.

“You’ll write to me?”

“If you like.”

“Not if I like. You must.”

“Very well.”

“Often?”

“Now and then.”

“As often as before.”

“No.”

The word surprised them both.

Anne stood quite still. A drop from the cedar struck the table with a soft ping. Behind her, Mr. Dove resumed his pursuit.

“Roo-coo-coo-coo.”

Mrs. Dove ran ahead, quick and light, while he followed with his breast puffed out, bowing until his beak nearly touched the path.

Reggie looked at them and then at Anne.

“I’d better go.”

This time she did not stop him.

He crossed the lawn. The wet grass brushed his shoes; the bright garden blurred at the edges, though he kept his eyes fiercely open. At the terrace he paused, hoping—idiotically, shamefully—that she would call. There was only the faint snip of a gardener’s shears beyond the wall.

He went through the drawing room. The blue parasol still lay upon the piano. In the hall, the maid appeared with his gloves.

“Good morning, sir.”

“Morning.”

Outside, the road shone exactly as before. That was the worst of roads and skies: nothing happened to them. A chap might have his entire future knocked flat, and the clouds went sailing on, the puddles glittered, the hedges smelt of briar. In a few minutes he would pass the hollyhocks. Then the bend. Then his mother’s house, where the bell would be rung and the dogs would stare and he would say he had had a pleasant visit.

He reached the gate.

“Reggie!”

His hand closed upon the latch.

No. He would not turn. She wanted him smiling, writing, talking nonsense, trotting after her while she laughed. She wanted yesterday without to-morrow. It wasn’t fair. For once Mr. Dove would keep walking.

“Reggie, please!”

He shut his eyes.

Then, softer, trembling and amused and unhappy all at once, her voice came across the wet lawn:

“Come back, Mr. Dove.”

He turned.

Anne stood beneath the cedar with one hand at her throat. She was smiling, but there were tears on her face. Behind her Mrs. Dove ran in a little circle, and Mr. Dove followed, bowing and bowing.

Reggie opened the gate, closed it again, and came back across the grass.

The Last Train to Bellwether

At eleven minutes past midnight, the last train arrived at Bellwether Station, though no train had been scheduled to stop there for twenty-three years.

Mara Venn was the only person who saw it.

She had been standing beneath the broken station clock, shaking rain from her umbrella, when a pale light appeared beyond the eastern bend. At first she thought it was a truck on the old service road. Then the rails began to hum under her boots.

The sound traveled through the abandoned platform, stirring scraps of paper and dust. A whistle called from the darkness—low, mournful, and impossibly near.

The train emerged without steam or smoke. Its black engine shone as if freshly painted, though silver moss clung to its wheels. Behind it came six passenger carriages, each glowing with amber light. Rain slid around the train but never seemed to touch it.

Mara stepped back.

For years, the railway authorities had promised to tear up the Bellwether line. For years, they had postponed it. The tracks remained, rusting among weeds, leading east into a tunnel blocked by a landslide and west toward a bridge that had collapsed before Mara was born.

Yet the train stopped with effortless precision.

A door opened.

A conductor in a midnight-blue uniform leaned out. He was an elderly man with a silver beard, a round cap, and eyes the gray-green color of the sea before a storm.

“Bellwether,” he announced. “One minute only.”

Mara stared at him.

The conductor checked a pocket watch. “Are you boarding, Miss Venn?”

She gripped the umbrella handle. “How do you know my name?”

“Your ticket.”

“I don’t have a ticket.”

He pointed to her coat pocket.

Mara almost laughed. Then she reached inside.

Her fingers closed around a rectangle of stiff paper.

It was cream-colored, edged in gold, and dry despite the rain. Printed across the center in faded green letters were the words:

MARA VENN  
BELLWETHER TO MORNING  
SINGLE JOURNEY  
NO RETURN

She looked up. “What does this mean?”

“Exactly what it says.”

“I’m not going anywhere.”

“Then why did you come to the station?”

Mara opened her mouth but found no answer.

She had lived in Bellwether all her life. She knew every narrow lane, every leaning chimney, every face in the bakery queue on winter mornings. She also knew the station was locked at night. The gate had been chained after local children began daring one another to sleep in the ticket office.

Still, at half past eleven, unable to remain in her silent house, she had found herself walking through the rain with her father’s old umbrella. The chain had been lying open on the ground. The station door had yielded at her touch.

She had told herself she needed air.

But the truth was that morning would bring the demolition crews to Venn’s Clockmakers, the little shop where her family had worked for four generations. The council had purchased the entire row to widen the road, and Mara had spent the day packing brass gears, cracked watch faces, invoices, tools, and clocks that no one wanted repaired.

At seven that evening, she had stopped the shop’s great regulator clock.

At eight, she had gone home.

At nine, she had realized she no longer knew who she was.

The conductor glanced at his watch again. “Thirty seconds.”

“Where does the train go?”

“To Morning.”

“That isn’t a place.”

“It is tonight.”

The rain thickened. Mara looked past him into the first carriage. It seemed warm inside. Dark wooden panels gleamed under brass lamps. A woman in a red scarf sat by one window, sleeping with her head against the glass.

“What happens if I stay?”

The conductor’s expression softened. “The usual things.”

Somewhere in town, a clock struck the quarter hour, though it was neither the hour nor the quarter.

Mara put one foot onto the train.

The conductor took her umbrella and folded it neatly. “Mind the gap.”

She boarded.

The door closed behind her, and Bellwether Station began to slide away.

Mara rushed to the window. The platform passed slowly at first—the broken clock, the peeling sign, the empty benches—then faster. Darkness swallowed everything.

“But the western bridge is gone,” she said.

The conductor handed back her umbrella. “Only during the day.”

The carriage held nine passengers.

The sleeping woman in the red scarf looked no older than twenty. Across from her sat a broad man wearing a baker’s apron powdered with flour. A boy in a green school blazer held a glass jar containing three fireflies. Near the rear door, twin sisters with white hair played cards on a suitcase.

No one seemed surprised to see Mara.

She chose an empty seat beside the window. The cushion sighed beneath her.

Outside, the night unrolled in impossible landscapes. The train crossed a bridge over a forest of silver trees. It ran along a black beach where enormous waves stood motionless beneath the moon. It passed a city composed entirely of lit windows, with no walls between them.

The conductor moved down the aisle, punching tickets. Each click of his silver punch sounded like a tiny lock closing.

When he reached Mara, he held out his hand.

She hesitated. “You said there’s no return.”

“There seldom is.”

“From Morning?”

“From any journey worth taking.”

She surrendered the ticket.

He inspected it, then frowned.

“Is something wrong?”

“It hasn’t printed your arrival time.”

“I didn’t print it.”

“No. You wouldn’t have.”

He punched a star-shaped hole in one corner and returned the ticket. “You’ll need to decide before the final stop.”

“Decide what?”

But he had already moved on.

The baker across the aisle leaned toward her.

“First journey?” he asked.

“Is it obvious?”

“You keep expecting explanations.”

His face was round and kind, though his eyes were swollen from recent tears. He carried a cardboard cake box on his knees.

“Where are you going?” Mara asked.

“To see my wife.”

“Does she live in Morning?”

“She lives nowhere now.”

Mara looked down.

The baker patted the cake box. “Forty-two years ago, I made her a birthday cake. Terrible thing. Burned at the edges, raw in the middle. I wrote her name in icing, but I was so nervous I misspelled it.”

“What did she say?”

“She married me.” He smiled. “Last week, I made the cake again. Perfectly this time. She died before she could taste it.”

“I’m sorry.”

“So am I.” He looked out at the moonlit sea. “I heard the train whistle last night. I knew she was calling. Or I wanted to know.”

“Will you be able to stay with her?”

The baker’s smile faded. “That’s what I intend to find out.”

The train entered a tunnel. The carriage lights dimmed.

For a moment, Mara saw her own reflection in the window: dark hair escaping its knot, tired eyes, rainwater on the collar of her coat. Then the glass brightened, and another reflection appeared beside hers.

Her father sat in the empty seat.

He looked as he had on the last morning of his life—thin, gray, and annoyed by illness. A magnifying lens was clipped over one eye.

“You’re holding it wrong,” he said.

Mara froze.

He reached toward her hands. Only then did she realize she was holding a tiny brass watch between her fingers.

It was the first watch he had taught her to repair.

“Thumb under the movement,” he said. “Not over it. You’ll bend the balance staff.”

She was twelve again, sitting at his workbench while rain tapped the shop windows.

“I can’t do it,” she heard herself say.

“You can.”

“The parts are too small.”

“Small things still matter.”

“That doesn’t make them easier.”

“No.” His smile appeared slowly. “But that is why we learn patience.”

The train burst from the tunnel.

The watch vanished. The seat beside Mara was empty.

She stood so quickly that her knee struck the table.

The conductor was at the far end of the carriage. Mara pushed past the card-playing twins and caught his sleeve.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing.”

“I saw my father.”

“Yes.”

“Was it him?”

The conductor considered. “Does it matter?”

“Of course it matters.”

“To the living, perhaps.”

Before Mara could answer, the train began to slow.

Beyond the windows lay a station lit by hundreds of candles. The sign on the platform read YESTERDAY.

“Five minutes,” the conductor called. “Passengers may disembark, but must return before the bell.”

The doors opened.

The baker rose, clutching his cake box. The woman in the red scarf woke with a gasp. The boy put the jar of fireflies in his pocket. All the passengers stepped onto the platform.

Mara remained seated.

The conductor paused by the door. “You may see him again.”

“My father?”

“If that is who you are looking for.”

“I’m not looking for him.”

“No?”

“He died six years ago. I know that.”

“Knowing a door is locked does not stop us from trying the handle.”

He stepped outside.

Mara followed.

Yesterday Station had no walls. Beyond the platform stood a field in summer sunlight, though the sky above the tracks remained midnight-black. Warm air moved through tall grass. Somewhere, unseen, bees hummed.

Paths led away from the platform, each marked by a wooden sign.

FIRST LOVE, read one.

LAST WORD.

THE DAY BEFORE.

IF ONLY.

Mara saw the baker hurrying down a path marked ONE MORE MEAL. The woman in the red scarf had chosen BEFORE I SAID YES. The schoolboy stood beneath a sign that read HOME AT FOUR O’CLOCK, unable to move.

Mara walked along the platform until she found a narrow path almost hidden by weeds.

THE SHOP, it said.

She followed.

The field vanished behind her. She smelled oil, dust, and metal. Then she was standing outside Venn’s Clockmakers on a winter evening six years earlier.

Every clock in the window showed a different time.

Through the glass, she saw her father at the workbench. He was bent over a carriage clock, his hands trembling as he fitted a gear into place.

Mara remembered this night.

She had been offered a position in Edinburgh by a company that restored museum clocks. It was everything she had once dreamed of: travel, difficult work, the chance to learn from masters of the trade. Her train left the following morning.

That evening, her father had collapsed in the shop.

The doctors found the illness. Mara canceled her journey. She told herself she would apply again next year, but next year brought hospital visits, then debts, then grief. After her father’s death, the shop became hers.

She had never left Bellwether.

Inside the memory, her younger self came down the stairs carrying a suitcase.

“I’ll miss the train,” Young Mara said.

Her father did not look up. “Then go.”

“You can barely hold the tweezers.”

“I’m tired.”

“You need a doctor.”

“I need to finish this clock.”

“You’re being stubborn.”

“So are you.”

Young Mara put down the suitcase. “I can catch the afternoon train.”

Her father’s hands stopped moving.

This was the moment Mara had replayed more than any other. If he had told her to go, she might have gone. If he had asked her to stay, she might have stayed without resentment.

Instead, he had said, “Do what you think is right.”

Mara had hated him for that answer.

She watched her younger self take off her coat.

Then she entered the shop.

Neither figure noticed her. She walked to the workbench and stood opposite her father.

“You knew,” she said.

His head remained bowed.

“You knew I wouldn’t leave if you were ill.”

Still he said nothing.

“You could have told me to go.”

The clocks ticked around them, hundreds of mechanical hearts refusing to beat together.

At last, her father looked up.

This time he saw her.

“I could have,” he said.

Mara forgot to breathe.

“Is this really you?”

He removed the magnifying lens. “You always ask questions when you are frightened.”

“You let me give up everything.”

“No.”

“I stayed for you.”

“You stayed because you loved me.”

“And what’s the difference?”

“Love is not a prison, Mara. But memory can be.”

The anger she had carried for six years rose into her throat.

“You left me with the shop. With the debts. With all those clocks no one cares about.”

“I left you my tools. You chose what to build with them.”

“I preserved everything.”

“Yes,” he said. “That was the trouble.”

A bell rang in the distance.

Mara turned toward the door.

“One minute,” called the conductor’s voice.

Her father picked up the tiny gear with his tweezers.

“What happens if I stay here?” she asked.

“We have this conversation again.”

“For how long?”

“For as long as you need to lose it entirely.”

She looked at the suitcase by the stairs. “I don’t know how to leave.”

“You already did.”

The station bell rang a second time.

Mara ran.

She raced back along the path, through the summer field, and onto the candlelit platform. The conductor stood beside the train.

“Wait!”

He held the door as she climbed aboard.

The baker had not returned.

Through the window, Mara saw him far out in the field, sitting at a table beneath an apple tree. A woman sat opposite him. Between them was a cake covered in white icing. He was laughing and crying at once.

The conductor rang his bell.

The train moved.

“Shouldn’t we wait for him?” Mara asked.

“He has made his choice.”

“He’ll be trapped there.”

“Perhaps. But not every trap feels cruel.”

The woman in the red scarf had returned. She sat upright, clutching her ticket in both hands. The schoolboy had returned too, but his jar was empty. The fireflies drifted over Yesterday Station as it disappeared behind them.

The baker’s abandoned seat still held a dusting of flour.

Mara sat beside the window.

She understood now why her ticket had no arrival time.

Morning was not merely a destination. It was a decision, and the train could not make it for her.

The journey continued.

They passed through stations called NEVER WAS, FORGOTTEN NAME, and JUST THIS ONCE. At each stop, one or two passengers left. Some returned before the bell. Some did not.

The white-haired twins stepped off at DIFFERENT ROADS, each walking in the opposite direction. The woman in the red scarf left at UNSPOKEN and came back without her scarf.

At last only Mara, the woman, and the schoolboy remained.

The sky outside began to lighten.

The conductor entered the carriage carrying a tray with three cups of tea. He gave one to each passenger and sat across from Mara.

“Final stop soon,” he said.

Mara wrapped her hands around the warm cup. “What is at Morning?”

“Whatever comes next.”

“That’s not very helpful.”

“The future rarely is, until it becomes the past.”

She took out her ticket. The blank space beneath the destination had begun to shimmer.

“What if I don’t know what I want?”

“You need only know what you refuse to keep carrying.”

Mara thought of the shop: the stopped regulator clock, the packed boxes, the dustless outline where her father’s coat had hung. She had believed preserving his life would preserve her love for him. Instead, every object had become evidence in a trial without a verdict.

“What do the others refuse to carry?” she asked.

The conductor glanced at the schoolboy, who was watching the empty jar.

“Guilt,” he said. Then he nodded toward the woman without the scarf. “A promise made to the wrong person.”

“And me?”

“You tell me.”

Outside, the horizon turned gold. The strange landscapes faded. Ordinary hills appeared, green with rain. Telephone poles ran beside the tracks. Sheep lifted their heads in morning fields.

Mara looked down at her ticket.

“I refuse,” she said slowly, “to spend the rest of my life waiting for the life I missed.”

The ticket grew warm.

Green letters appeared in the blank space:

ARRIVAL: 6:12 A.M.

The conductor smiled.

The whistle sounded.

Ahead stood Bellwether Station.

But it was not the station Mara had boarded from. Sunlight shone on new glass shelters. The old ticket office had become a café. Flower boxes hung beneath the restored clock, which displayed the correct time.

On the opposite platform, commuters waited with phones and briefcases. A bright red train stood beneath a sign reading:

NORTHBOUND—EDINBURGH—6:20

Mara stared.

“This isn’t my Bellwether.”

“It can be.”

“What year is it?”

“Morning.”

The train stopped.

The schoolboy was first to leave. On the platform, a middle-aged woman cried out and dropped her handbag. She ran to him, and he ran into her arms.

The woman who had worn the red scarf stepped down next. A younger woman waited beside the café, holding two coffees and smiling nervously.

Mara remained in her seat.

“What if I get off and everything disappears?” she asked.

The conductor opened the door. “Everything disappears, Miss Venn. That is no reason to remain seated.”

She stepped onto the platform.

Cold morning air filled her lungs.

When she turned, the black train was already moving. The conductor leaned from the doorway and touched two fingers to the brim of his cap.

“Mind the gap,” he called.

Then the train passed into sunlight and was gone.

Mara stood alone.

The station slowly changed around her.

The glass shelters faded. The café became the locked ticket office. The flower boxes vanished, and the clock cracked across its face. The opposite platform emptied. The red northbound train dissolved into mist.

For one terrible moment, Mara thought the journey had changed nothing.

Then she heard a diesel engine.

A demolition van stopped outside the station. Two workers climbed out, arguing about where to find coffee. Beyond them, Bellwether woke beneath a pale sky.

Mara checked her phone.

6:12 a.m.

She walked home.

At nine, the demolition crew arrived at Venn’s Clockmakers. Their supervisor found Mara waiting outside beside twelve sealed boxes and the great regulator clock.

“You’re cutting it close,” he said. “We need the building empty.”

“It is.”

“You taking that clock?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

Mara looked down the road.

She had made three calls since returning home. The first was to a railway company. The second was to an old friend in Edinburgh. The third was to the council officer overseeing the abandoned station.

“For now,” she said, “across town.”

Six months later, Bellwether Station reopened.

Not for trains—the line remained broken in both directions—but as a workshop, café, and small museum. The restored sign above the entrance read:

Venn’s Clockmakers  
Repairs, Restorations, and Departures

Mara placed her workbench in the old ticket office. She taught classes on Saturdays and repaired clocks during the week. Once a month, she traveled to Edinburgh to assist with the museum collection. She became skilled at leaving and, more importantly, at returning without mistaking return for surrender.

The great regulator clock stood on the platform beneath the broken station clock, which Mara never repaired.

Visitors sometimes asked why.

“One correct clock is useful,” she would say. “Two only start an argument.”

Years passed.

On a rainy evening in late October, Mara was closing the workshop when she found a boy waiting beneath the platform lamps. He wore a green school blazer of an old-fashioned cut.

At first she did not recognize him.

Then he held up a glass jar. Three fireflies glowed inside.

“You were on the train,” Mara said.

“So were you.”

He had not aged.

Mara set down her keys.

“Are you here to take me back?”

“No.” He placed the jar on the bench. “The conductor asked me to deliver this.”

Inside the jar, beneath the fireflies, lay a cream-colored ticket edged in gold.

Mara did not touch it.

“What does it say?”

The boy smiled. “Not yet.”

A whistle called in the distance.

The rails, red with rust and buried beneath weeds, began to hum.

Mara looked toward the eastern bend. A pale light moved behind the trees, though the tunnel beyond them was still sealed with stone.

“Who is the ticket for?” she asked.

The boy pointed toward the station entrance.

A woman stood there, soaked by the rain. She was perhaps twenty years old and wore a red scarf. She looked exhausted and frightened.

“Is this Bellwether?” the woman asked.

Mara glanced at the clock.

It was eleven minutes past midnight.

She took her father’s umbrella from the stand, walked to the platform edge, and opened it over the stranger.

“Yes,” Mara said as the last train approached. “But only for one minute.”
